new_statements.quote: Stress in Tena Quichua generally falls on the penultimate syllable (as shown in the examples in (1) above). However, a subset of suffixes causes stress to fall on the last syllable of the word, including: the locative (LOC) suffix when added to polysyllabic words ending in a vowel (see example (5) above), third person singular /-n/ and plural /-nun/ present tense markers (see examples (6) above and (7)), and the suffix /-nɡax/ used to express future obligation (see example (8)). [...] There are also cases in which the addition of a suffix does not cause stress shift to the new penultimate syllable, as in the topic marker (TOP) /-ɡa/ (Orr 1991).

new_statements.relation_note: NOT in the READALL works list for this item; it was downloaded by the 2026-09-16 pass (see in our check folder) and lies inside the custody tree, so it was read here as the only openable Tena Quichua source. It agrees with the catalog's penultimate rule (penultimate stress) and refines it with the suffix-conditioned final-stress class, the extrametrical topic marker, variable accusative behaviour, and initial/second-syllable secondary stress. Describes exactly the tena1240 variety (Tena Quichua, quw, Napo above the Coca, Misahualli/Arajuno/Ansuc tributaries).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word by default. A closed set of suffixes attracts stress to the final syllable: the locative /-i/ on polysyllabic vowel-final words (/ˈjaku-i/ > [jaˈkw-i] 'in the water'), the third-person present markers /-n/ (sg) and /-nun/ (pl) (/tiɡra-ˈnun/ 'they turn'), and the future-obligation suffix /-nɡax/ (/piti-nˈɡa-x/ 'in order to cut'). Some suffixes are extrametrical, i.e. adding them does not move stress to the new penult: the topic marker /-ɡa/ (citing Orr 1991) and, variably, the accusative /-ɾa/ (/ˈkwika-ɾa/ 'earthworm-ACC' vs /aiˈtʃa-ɾa/ 'meat-ACC').
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 113: 'Last, there are some words where secondary stress may be perceived, either on the first or sometimes second syllable, as in (12) and (13).' Examples: /ˌjanapa-ɾj-aˈnun/ 'they are helping', /aˌʃanɡa-ˈɡuna/ 'baskets'; Figure 4 (p. 114) shows secondary stress on the initial syllable with penultimate primary stress in [ˌrimanuˈnau̯ka] 'they were talking to each other'. The authors call for an acoustic study; preliminary observation is that intensity and an f0 peak mark the stressed syllable and unstressed vowels are not reduced.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress with the locative /-i/, 3sg /-n/, 3pl /-nun/ and /-nɡax/; no shift with the topic marker /-ɡa/ and variably with the accusative /-ɾa/ ('Whether or not penultimate stress is observed with /-ɾa/ may be due to several factors, including word order and placement within the discourse'). The authors state that 'more work on stress (and stress shift) in TQ is needed' (p. 114).
new_statements.identity_note: O'Rourke & Swanson 2013 describe Tena Quichua (ISO 639-3 quw), 'spoken in the Eastern Amazonian region of Ecuador on the Napo River above the mouth of the Rio Coca, primarily on three tributaries: the Misahualli, the Arajuno, and the Ansuc' (p. 107), i.e. the tena1240 variety itself, distinguished from Napo Quichua and Pastaza (Bobonaza) Quichua. Orr 1992 Runa shimi is a grammar of the same Tena variety per its title; its content could not be verified.

new_statements.quote: Yachaujcunara tapungui: Runa shimira rimausha, maican uyaricta mas shinzhi uyarin? Puchucai Ñaupajpi Uyarij. Chi parti mas shinzhi uyarij an, chimanda chi uyarijta mishu shimíi grave ninaun. [...] Runa shimíi ñalla tucui shimiunara Puchucai Ñaupajpi Uyarijta mas shinzhi rimanchi, casna: qui-hua, in-di, ta-ru-ga, ri-cun-chi-mi, ma-qui-sa-pa-ra, a-pi-mush-can-gui-chu. Tucui chi shimiunara puchucai uyarij ñaupajpi mas shinzhi rimanchi. [Lección 8:] (Puchucaibi mas shinzhi uyarijca mishu shimíi aguda ninaun). Quillcara ricushcái mana pandangáj chi shimiunái á, í, ú quillcanara ushangui, casna: micuushcái, paihuáj, pujlláun, rimangáj, callpanáun, ucúi.
new_statements.translation: Ask the students: when speaking Quichua, which syllable sounds strongest? The syllable before the last. That part is the strongest syllable; hence in Spanish that syllable(-stress) is called 'grave'. [...] In Quichua we pronounce almost all words with the next-to-last syllable strongest, thus: QUI-hua, IN-di, ta-RU-ga, ri-cun-CHI-mi, ma-qui-sa-PA-ra, a-pi-mush-can-GUI-chu (stressed syllables bold in the original). All those words we say with the syllable before the last strongest. [Lesson 8:] (When the last syllable sounds strongest, in Spanish it is called 'aguda'.) So that the reader is not confused, á, í, ú can be written in those words, thus: micuushcái, paihuáj, pujlláun, rimangáj, callpanáun, ucúi.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog records penultimate stress for all lengths (penultimate stress); Orr states the same default ('ñalla tucui shimiunara' = almost all words, penult) and adds two exception classes the catalog does not record: lexical/suffixal final stress (aguda forms in -áj, -áun, -ái, -úi) and non-shifting enclitics -ga/-mi yielding antepenultimate stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable in almost all words, regardless of length (examples of 2 to 6 syllables, all penult-stressed, including suffixed verb forms such as ricunchimi, apimushcanguichu). Two marked classes are taught as exceptions and written with an accent mark: 'agudas' with final stress (micuushcái, paihuáj, pujlláun, rimangáj, callpanáun, ucúi — forms ending in -j/-un/-i suffixes) and 'esdrújulas' with antepenultimate stress, which arise when topic -ga or evidential -mi is added and stress stays put (yáyaga, mámaga, állcuga, rimáshaga, ríjpiga, cújpiga, chimándami, raushcaráicumi). The Spanish preface (front matter p. [iv]) summarises: 'El tema de las lecciones 6 a 8 es el uso de la tilde.. se ejemplifican los términos grave (7), aguda y esdrújula (8).' The Quichua-Spanish glossary (p. 58) restates: 'Puchucai ñaupajpi uyarij mas shinzhi uyarin - Acento grave'.
new_statements.exceptions: Final-stressed (aguda) words marked with written accent: micuushcái, paihuáj, pujlláun, rimangáj, callpanáun, ucúi; antepenult-stressed (esdrújula) words when enclitic -ga (topic) or -mi (evidential) is attached without shifting stress: yáyaga, mámaga, állcuga, rimáshaga, ríjpiga, cújpiga, chimándami, raushcaráicumi.
new_statements.identity_note: Orr's grammar is explicitly for the Quichua of the Tena and Arajuno sectors (upper Napo down to the mouth of the Suno), which she distinguishes from the lower Napo/Sucumbíos dialect and the Pastaza/Bobonaza dialect; this is the tena1240 variety (ISO quw), so no identity mismatch.

The deciding source is a 1991 pedagogical lesson book (20-page excerpt), which is not the best available description, but the two better sources — O'Rourke & Swanson 2013 (JIPA Illustration, downloaded now, pp.113-114) and Grzech 2016 (SOAS PhD grammar sketch, already held, §2.1.2.2 p.44, pitch-track-checked) — both state that Tena Quichua stress falls on the penultimate syllable by default, so the penultimate (non-strict, word-domain) coding stands.
